strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: lifting concept bottleneck-style interpretability from global image-level representations to a spatially grounded, foundation-model setting, enabling concept-based explanations for classification, captioning, steering, and open-vocabulary segmentation — a combination not previously demonstrated.

Comprehensive and multi-faceted evaluation: quantitative interpretability metrics (locality, consistency, impurity, C2-score) on part-annotated benchmarks, large-scale MTurk user studies with control questions and quality filtering (~1000 concepts, 5 annotators each), an LLM-judge naming evaluation with per-method random baselines, and downstream task comparisons against strong recent baselines (DN-CBM, MSAE, PatchSAE, SALF-CBM, multiple CBMs, CLIP-DINOiser).

Strong downstream results: CFM matches its opaque backbone (CLIP-DINOiser) on open-vocabulary segmentation across 8 benchmarks while providing concept-level explanations for every segment, and achieves competitive classification accuracy versus CBMs trained specifically for that task.

Technically sound core: the insight that Matryoshka dictionary vectors are residual by design, and therefore need hierarchy-aware reconstruction for accurate naming, is well argued and supported (Fig. B1); co-occurrence-based hierarchy discovery avoids imposing external taxonomies.

Excellent reproducibility posture: the appendix provides full training details, losses, hyperparameters, user-study protocols, judge prompts, and extensive ablations (dictionary size, BatchTopK k, Matryoshka fractions), plus code availability and honest discussion of limitations (e.g., naming imperfections in Fig. C5).
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on combining existing components (CLIP-DINOiser features, Matryoshka SAEs, BatchTopK, AnyUp upsampling, prior naming procedures); while the integration is non-trivial and effective, the individual technical novelty is moderate.

The hierarchy discovery threshold τ=0.75 and the naming coefficient α=1.33 are chosen empirically/qualitatively rather than via a principled or quantitatively validated procedure; sensitivity to these hyperparameters is not ablated.

Some inconsistency between the main text and appendix: Eq. (3)/(4) in the main paper (argmin over cosine, unweighted parent sum) differs from the formal procedure in B.4/B.8 (argmax, weighted ancestors with mean activations and α); this should be reconciled, though it does not undermine the results.

Concept naming remains imperfect (e.g., generic or incorrect fine-grained names in Fig. C5, 'small resolution'-type concepts), acknowledged by the authors, so claims about 'meaningful' names should be read with the reported error rates in mind.

Reliance on a proprietary LLM judge (gpt-5-mini) for naming accuracy introduces potential evaluator bias and reduces reproducibility, although MTurk results and the SBERT similarity analysis partially mitigate this.
Scale is limited: only CLIP ViT-B/16 trained on CC12M; no evidence the approach scales to larger backbones or whether hierarchies/naming quality degrade at larger dictionary sizes beyond 16k.

The captioning result (identical CLIP-Score to the backbone, 0.72 vs 0.72) shows parity rather than improvement, and steering is demonstrated mainly qualitatively without a quantitative measure of steering effectiveness (e.g., caption change metrics or human verification).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: prior concept-bottleneck approaches for foundation models (DN-CBM, MSAE, SpLiCE) operate on global, image-level features, limiting them to classification. Lifting concept decompositions to patch-level, spatially grounded representations that remain compatible with dense downstream tasks (open-vocabulary segmentation, captioning) is a meaningful and useful contribution to concept-based interpretability.

Evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: quantitative interpretability metrics (locality, consistency, impurity, C2-Score) on part-annotated data, comparisons against both spatially-aware (PatchSAE, SALF-CBM) and post-hoc-attributed baselines (LRP over DN-CBM/MSAE, App. C.5), three large-scale MTurk user studies with control questions and quality filtering, an LLM-judge naming evaluation with per-method random baselines, downstream results on classification, OVS across 8 benchmarks, and captioning parity with steering demonstrations.

The hierarchy discovery (patch-level co-occurrence, Eq. 2) and hierarchy-aware concept vector reconstruction (Eq. 4, Fig. B1) are well-motivated: the observation that Matryoshka dictionary vectors are residual and thus misnamed in isolation is a real, well-diagnosed problem, and the fix is simple and validated by the naming studies.

The expanded, concreteness-filtered, part-of-speech-aware vocabulary construction (App. B.4) is a non-trivial practical contribution that the authors show matters for fine-grained labeling, and the appendix provides enough detail (training objectives, hyperparameters, ablations over dictionary size and sparsity) to support reproducibility.
Limitations are honestly discussed, including imperfect naming (Fig. C5) and the difficulty of evaluating unsupervised concept explanations.
weaknesses: Core methodological novelty is limited. The approach is a careful combination of existing components: Matryoshka SAE [6], BatchTopK [5], CLIP-DINOiser-style DINOised features [72], and AnyUp [70]. The genuinely new elements (co-occurrence-based parent-child discovery, hierarchy-aware naming, vocabulary construction) are relatively shallow: a thresholded conditional-probability matrix and a weighted sum of parent dictionary vectors with an empirically chosen coefficient alpha = 1.33. The paper's value is more integration/engineering than conceptual advance.

Some evaluation framing overstates the contribution. The OVS results (Tab. 1) essentially match CLIP-DINOiser, which is unsurprising since CFM builds directly on it and applies AnyUp; the 'on par with strongest baselines' claim is really 'the SAE bottleneck costs almost nothing,' which is valuable but should be presented as such. A clearer decomposition of where the segmentation performance comes from (DINOised features vs. SAE vs. AnyUp) is missing.

Concerns about evaluation fairness and circularity: (a) CFM uses an extra DINO model for feature smoothing, which baselines do not, so part of the locality/consistency gains may come from the backbone enhancement rather than the concept extraction; (b) the naming-quality judge (gpt-5-mini) may favor CFM's vocabulary style, and judging 'concept presence' is a weaker test than judging whether the name is the *right* name for the activating region; (c) captioning steering examples rely on Google-Gemini to select which concepts to intervene on (Fig. C15), which weakens the claim that the concept space itself is interpretable and controllable without an external model.

Technical sloppiness that should have been caught: Eq. (3) and Eq. (4) use argmin over cosine similarity, which contradicts Eq. (B.9)'s argmax and would select the most dissimilar label; the caption in Fig. 3 mixes concepts of 'naming' into a figure about consistency/grounding; Fig. A4's caption labels (a)/(b) inconsistently with its description. Also, 'sets a new standard' and 'the first concept-based foundation model' are strong claims given concurrent works (e.g., PatchSAE is already local; hierarchical SAEs already exist).

Scale and generality are limited: a single ViT-B/16 backbone, one dataset (CC12M) for SAE training, and hard-coded hyperparameters (tau = 0.75 validated only 'qualitatively', alpha = 1.33 'empirically chosen'). The claimed status as a 'foundation model' would be more convincing with evidence at larger backbone/dictionary scales or on a second backbone family, and with a sensitivity analysis for the hierarchy threshold rather than qualitative validation.

The classification comparison (Fig. 6) mixes training recipes: CFM is a frozen-backbone linear probe while several baselines are concept classifiers trained specifically for the task; the claim of 'competitive' performance is fine, but the paper should more carefully acknowledge that CFM is not trying to win here, and the bolded 'best' formatting over CFM's 55.4 on Places (vs. DN-CBM's 55.1) risks reading as a head-to-head win that the setup does not support.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing concept-based interpretability methods for VLMs (DN-CBM, MSAE, SpLiCE) are limited to global image-level representations and classification, whereas CFM extends concept decompositions to spatially grounded, patch-level representations applicable to diverse downstream tasks (classification, captioning, open-vocabulary segmentation). This positioning is clearly argued and well supported.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: quantitative locality/consistency/impurity metrics on PartImageNet and COCO-Stuff with adapted baselines, the annotation-free C2-Score, three large-scale MTurk user studies (with control questions and quality filtering described in detail), an automated GPT-judge evaluation with per-method random baselines, and downstream benchmarks on 8 segmentation datasets.

CFM matches its opaque backbone on open-vocabulary segmentation (Tab. 1, on par with CLIP-DINOiser) and captioning (Fig. 7) while providing explanations — a strong empirical demonstration that interpretability does not come at a performance cost in the foundation-model setting.

The hierarchy discovery (Eq. 2) and hierarchy-aware naming (Eq. 4 / B.8) are sensible, data-driven contributions that address a real failure mode (residual Matryoshka dictionary vectors yielding erroneous labels like 'Inspiron'), and the naming improvements are demonstrated with statistical significance and against random-concept baselines.

The appendix is exemplary for reproducibility: full training details, hyperparameter sweeps, ablations over dictionary size and sparsity (Tabs. B1–B3), user study instructions, judge prompts, and honest limitation examples (e.g., Fig. C5 shows hierarchies where naming fails).
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily in integration rather than new methods: the backbone (CLIP-DINOiser), sparsity objective (BatchTopK), hierarchical SAE (Matryoshka), and upsampling (AnyUp) are all existing components. The genuinely new pieces — patch-wise co-occurrence hierarchy discovery and hierarchy-aware naming — are relatively simple heuristics (conditional co-occurrence thresholding; parent-offset vector matching). The contributions are well executed, but reviewers seeking algorithmic novelty may find the technical depth modest.

The ablation of the naming contribution is confounded: CFM uses a much larger, concreteness-filtered, template-conditioned vocabulary (Sec. B.4) than baselines, and the paper itself notes prior vocabularies are 'too limited'. It is unclear how much of the naming improvement (Fig. 5) comes from the hierarchy-aware naming scheme vs. simply the enlarged vocabulary; an ablation isolating Eq. 4 from the vocabulary change would substantially strengthen the case.

Several hyperparameters are set by qualitative validation rather than principled criteria (τ=0.75 for hierarchy edges, α=1.33 for naming offset, the six Matryoshka shell ratios), which raises concerns about fragility and reproducibility of the hierarchy quality results, despite the authors' claim that τ transfers across SAEs.

There are internal inconsistencies in the equations: Eq. 3 and Eq. 4 in the main text use argmin over cosine similarity while the appendix (B.9, B.12) uses argmax for the same procedure — presumably a sign error that should be corrected; Eq. 2's numerator/denominator indexing (Cij as 'probability of i given j' with Ajp in the denominator) also reads ambiguously.

Interpretability claims rest partly on LLM judges (gpt-5-mini for concept presence, Google-Gemini for selecting steering concepts), whose reliability for judging fine-grained visual concepts is not validated (e.g., against human agreement), and the steering results are qualitative only — no quantitative steering fidelity metric is reported.

Classification accuracy, while competitive, is not state-of-the-art (78.9 vs. 79.5 for DN-CBM on ImageNet), and the benefit of the hierarchy for actual downstream decision quality (rather than explanation quality) is not directly quantified — e.g., no experiment showing hierarchy-aware explanations improve human task performance or steering control accuracy.
